posts.title: Keeping a starter honest
posts.excerpt: Observations on feeding ratios, jar marks and the day-to-day behaviour of a school starter.
posts.content:
Every jar on the shelf carries a rubber band at the level of the last feed. By six o'clock the band tells the story of the night: how far the starter rose, whether it has begun to fall, and how much flour it will need.

Amara Osei asks students to write that level down before they touch anything. The habit is dull and it is the one that matters most when a bakery runs ten starters at once.

posts.title: Reading a croissant crumb
posts.excerpt: What an open honeycomb tells you about butter temperature, folds and proof.
posts.content:
Cut a croissant in half and the whole morning is visible: the evenness of the layers, the size of the holes, the colour of the walls. Tomás Ferreira reads crumb the way a mechanic reads a spark plug.

Students cut one on Friday at the crumb critique and write down two things to change on Monday.

posts.title: What is in the storeroom
posts.excerpt: Flour sacks, grain bins and the quiet arithmetic of ordering for twelve benches.
posts.content:
A cohort of twelve gets through more flour than anyone expects. Lukas Brenner keeps the storeroom list on one sheet: what arrived, what was used, what is left for Friday.

Ordering is part of the course. Students take a turn at the list in week five.

posts.title: The knife roll
posts.excerpt: Why every student leaves with a lame, a scraper, a thermometer and a blank notebook.
posts.content:
The knife roll is handed out on the first Monday. Inside are a lame, a bench scraper, a dough thermometer and a pencil, with a notebook beside it.

By the last week the notebook is full of formulas, temperatures and corrections, which is why we call it the bench book.
